plan.contextChunk: This figure shows three rendered orbital shapes in a row on a white background, each captioned in bold beneath it, reading from left to right "An s orbital", "A p orbital", and "A d orbital". The leftmost is one translucent pink sphere, smooth and unbroken in every direction, with a small yellow-green bead at its center marking the nucleus. The middle shape stacks two lobes vertically, a rounded pink one above and a matching blue one below, meeting at a green nucleus bead; both are drawn as full, doorknob-like volumes rather than pointed teardrops, and they pinch away to nothing where they meet. The rightmost carries four lobes in a cloverleaf around a central green bead, their colors alternating around the ring: pink at the upper left and lower right, blue at the upper right and lower left. Color does the encoding, pink and blue standing for opposite algebraic signs of the wave function across a node, so the alternation shows the sign flipping with each crossing from one lobe to the next. The three together set out the orbital shapes and sign patterns that later account for bonding.

elements: white background matching the source figure
single centered selected orbital display, replacing the original three-panel row through a toggle
caption below the selected orbital in bold black text: 'An s orbital', 'A p orbital', or 'A d orbital'
central nucleus bead at the origin, small yellow-green glossy sphere visible in front of the orbital surfaces
s orbital: one translucent smooth pink sphere centered on the nucleus
p orbital: two vertically stacked rounded lobes pinched to zero at the nucleus, pink lobe above and blue lobe below
p orbital nodal gap: horizontal node through the nucleus separating the upper and lower lobes
d orbital: four rounded cloverleaf lobes arranged in the screen plane around the nucleus
d orbital upper-left pink lobe
d orbital upper-right blue lobe
d orbital lower-left blue lobe
d orbital lower-right pink lobe
d orbital nodal gaps: vertical and horizontal cross-shaped empty space through the nucleus
click-selection highlight outline or glow on the clicked lobe
same-sign highlight state that brightens all lobes sharing the clicked lobe color and dims opposite-sign lobes

interactions.label: Orbital
interactions.teaches: Comparing s, p, and d in the same central position makes the increase in lobe count and node structure clear: s has no node, p has one sign change, and d alternates signs across two nodes
Pink and blue are opposite algebraic signs of the wave function; selecting one lobe shows that separated lobes with the same color belong to the same sign region
The orbital pictures are three-dimensional volumes rather than flat petals; rotating the selected orbital reveals the spatial extent around the nucleus

demo_steps.title: s orbital
demo_steps.narration: The s orbital is a single spherical region surrounding the nucleus. Because there is only one continuous pink region, no sign-changing node cuts through it.

demo_steps.title: p orbital
demo_steps.narration: The p orbital has two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus. The pink and blue halves show opposite signs, separated by a nodal plane through the nucleus.

demo_steps.title: d orbital
demo_steps.narration: The d orbital has four lobes arranged as a cloverleaf. The colors alternate around the center, so crossing each node flips the sign of the wave function.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a front-on camera so the p orbital reads as a vertical dumbbell and the d orbital reads as a four-lobed clover, matching the source image. World-space scale: selected orbital should fit inside about 3.0 units wide by 2.6 units tall; nucleus at (0,0,0) with radius 0.11. s orbital: sphere radius about 1.05 centered at origin, translucent pink #d98592 with opacity about 0.58. p orbital: vertical axis along +Y; upper pink lobe centered visually around y=+0.62, lower blue lobe centered around y=-0.62; each lobe about 1.35 wide in X, 1.05 tall in Y, 0.95 deep in Z, pinched/tapered to the nucleus at y=0. The p nodal plane is the horizontal XZ plane through the origin, visible as the clean gap where the two lobes meet. d orbital: four lobes lie mainly in the XY screen plane, centers approximately at (-0.55,+0.55), (+0.55,+0.55), (-0.55,-0.55), and (+0.55,-0.55), each about 0.82 radius, rounded and slightly bulbous, tapering inward toward the nucleus. d colors alternate: upper-left pink #d98592, upper-right blue #238bd0, lower-left blue #238bd0, lower-right pink #d98592. The d nodal planes appear as the vertical YZ plane and horizontal XZ plane through the nucleus, producing a cross-shaped empty gap. Nucleus material: glossy yellow-green #72b84a with small pale highlight #d7c76a. Captions sit about 1.45 units below the nucleus, bold black, matching the source wording exactly: 'An s orbital', 'A p orbital', 'A d orbital', with the orbital letter italicized if text rendering supports mixed style.
interactionPlan.notes: Model lobes as smooth implicit/metaball surfaces or high-resolution superquadric/parametric meshes rather than simple ellipsoids, because the source lobes are rounded at the outside but narrow toward the nucleus. Use transparent physical materials with high roughness and soft studio lighting to reproduce the glassy textbook-rendered look. Store each lobe mesh with userData.sign = 'pink' or 'blue'; click raycasting should brighten all meshes with the same sign and dim opposite-sign meshes. On orbitalType changes, crossfade or slide the selected orbital into the center rather than showing all three full panels at once. Keep orbit controls enabled but initialize and reset to the exact front-on view used by the source.

authoredContext:
What do orbitals look like? There are four different kinds of orbitals, denoted s, p, d, and f, each with a different shape. Of the four, we’ll be concerned primarily with s and p orbitals because these are the most common in organic and biological chemistry. An s orbital has a spherical shape, with the nucleus at its center; a p orbital has a dumbbell shape with two parts, or lobes; and four of the five d orbitals have a cloverleaf shape with four lobes, as shown in the figure. The fifth d orbital is shaped like an elongated dumbbell with a doughnut around its middle.

The three different p orbitals within a given shell are oriented in space along mutually perpendicular directions, denoted px, py, and pz. As shown in the figure, the two lobes of each p orbital are separated by a region of zero electron density called a node. Furthermore, the two orbital regions separated by the node have different algebraic signs, + and −, in the wave function, as represented by the different colors in the figure and the figure. As we’ll see in Section 1.11, these algebraic signs for different orbital lobes have important consequences with respect to chemical bonding and chemical reactivity.

Representations of s, p, and d orbitals. An s orbital is spherical, a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, and four of the five d orbitals are cloverleaf-shaped. Different lobes of p orbitals are often drawn for convenience as teardrops, but their actual shape is more like that of a doorknob, as indicated.

A characteristic s, p, and d orbital with the nucleus at the center of each. Two cloverleaf-shaped lobes and four cloverleaf-shaped lobes form the p and d orbitals, respectively.

The orbitals in an atom are organized into different layers around the nucleus called electron shells, which are centered around the nucleus and have successively larger size and energy. Different shells contain different numbers and kinds of orbitals, and each orbital within a shell can be occupied by two electrons. The first shell contains only a single s orbital, denoted 1s, and thus holds only 2 electrons. The second shell contains one 2s orbital and three 2p orbitals and thus holds a total of 8 electrons. The third shell contains a 3s orbital, three 3p orbitals, and five 3d orbitals, for a total capacity of 18 electrons. These orbital groupings and their energy levels are shown in the figure.

discrepancies: The source presents the s, p, and d orbitals side-by-side for direct comparison, while the generated figure shows only one orbital at a time through toggles.
The generated default view is dominated by a single enlarged s orbital, so the overall three-panel composition of the source is not reproduced at first glance.
The lobe shapes are somewhat idealized and uniform compared with the softer, slightly flattened and organic-looking lobes in the source.
The generated colors are more saturated and glossy, especially the blue lobes, whereas the source uses softer translucent pastel shading.
The nucleus/highlight treatment is more elaborate than the small simple green center marker in the source.
evaluation.notes: The orbital primitives, colors, captions, and sign relationships are mostly correct, but the source's side-by-side comparison layout is replaced by a one-at-a-time interactive view.
action_items: Add an optional or default comparison view showing the s, p, and d orbitals side-by-side with their captions, matching the source composition.
Soften the material colors and reduce glossiness to better match the translucent textbook rendering.
Adjust p and d lobe proportions to be slightly more flattened and organic like the reference lobes.
Make the nucleus appear as a smaller, simpler green marker without the extra prominent highlight bead.
